blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: May it please your Lordship, may we call Dr Saladi, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR SATYANARAYANA SALADI (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you state your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Satyanarayana Murthy Saladi.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Dr Saladi, could you confirm that as of the summer of 2015 you were a consultant paediatrician based at the Countess of Chester Hospital?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And you understand, I anticipate, that you have been invited here today to answer questions about a baby in the neonatal unit by the name of [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Is it right that you were on annual leave when [Baby F] and his twin brother [Baby E] were born on 29 July 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: However, a few days later, on the 4th going into 5 August 2015, you returned to work and you were designated the paediatrician of the week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Could you explain to the jury in a sentence or two what that means?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Paediatrician of the week is a system where we, as the consultants, sort of oversee the care of the babies who are admitted to the children's ward as well as the neonatal unit for that week. And if I remember correctly, at that time it used to start from Friday and continued until the next Friday morning.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. We understand, and we've already heard, that your colleague, Dr John Gibbs, was the paediatrician of the week at the point the boys were born.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Possibly.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. So when you came into the hospital on the 4th or 5 August, were you appraised, brought up to speed, with all the relevant information pertaining to the babies who would be under your general management --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- and clinical control?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did that include [Baby F]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Did you conduct what is referred to as a grand round on the morning of 4 August 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And we're going to look at the clinical notes that were created as part of that grand round. They'll appear on the
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: screen just to your right there. They are behind tile number 67, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You'll see from that representation there that these were notes made by a junior colleague of yours, Dr Gail Beech. Is the process that the registrar writes up the notes when conducting the grand round in the company of the paediatrician of the week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So if we can look at Dr Gail Beech's notes, please, of the weekly neonatal unit to be completed every Thursday.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Tuesday.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Tuesday, apologies. Dated 4 August. The gestational age of the baby. He was now in his seventh day of life.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The named consultant, Dr Gibbs. And then paediatrician of the week, yourself. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So this is prepared on the 4th.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. So would this be the process: Dr Beech noting any observations made by you and the information provided to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have seen the baby on 5th and these -- this document is prepared a day before.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because, basically, grand round is -- basically we look at all the information so they prepare all this information on the day before so that we have all that information at hand. So I wouldn't have seen the baby on 4 August.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But I would have seen this information on 5 August.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes. So the information is prepared by a junior doctor and provided to you in advance of your attending upon the baby —
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: On 5 August.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- on 5 August?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And prior to coming to court to give evidence, have you had the opportunity to refresh your memory as to the contents of the notes that we've put on screen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Does it accord with your recollection of this baby and the information --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- collected about him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: We can see there, if we look to the right, that, amongst other information recorded, was the fact that hyperglycaemia had resolved.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Could you confirm that hyperglycaemia refers to an elevated blood sugar level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: This baby's hyperglycaemia resolved, do you recall, within a day or two of his birth?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is...
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And did it require any further treatment, the hyperglycaemia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There was -- the baby did receive insulin for a very short period to control the hyperglycaemia in the first couple of days of life.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could scroll down, please, and continue to scroll down, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now we move to the grand round itself on 5 August.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you having been appraised all of the relevant information, you undertook this round and you created a plan for the continuing care of this baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Looking at the plan, the first stage was an abdominal Xray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, because what is said happened on the fourth night, my entire round was written again on this document and this plan is part of that plan. So it would be there in the subsequent pages.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. The events of the previous night, were they reported to you through Dr Harkness; do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: You can't recall. If we could just leave this tile then and go to tile 187, please, Mr Murphy, and the document behind it, please, which should be J2933.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see an entry from the registrar Dr Harkness recorded at 03.30 hours on 5 August.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So that's overnight --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- and prior to your grand round? We can see what it is that Dr Harkness recorded as to the events in the early hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: For your information, Dr Saladi, the jury have already heard from Dr Harkness --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- and heard his account of these. But if you care to refresh your memory of Dr Harkness' notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)
Continue to scroll down, please, Mr Murphy.
So we can see that amongst other notes made by Dr Harkness, at the bottom of our page he, Dr Harkness, has documented the plan to continue to monitor sugars.
Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: If we could then return, please, Mr Murphy, to the grand round note, which was behind tile 67.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the plan that you devised during the grand round, was that based, at least in part, on the events of the early hours, as recorded by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So having reminded yourself of Dr Harkness' notes, could you take us through the plan and your thinking behind it, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Can I ask you to go through my actual rounds, which is there, two pages down below?
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right. So you want to look at page 2932?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I wonder whether --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I will be able to tell you when, if you go down.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: If we could scroll up.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He wants to go down, he wants to go further on from there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I want to go down to the next pages after Dr Harkness' notes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder whether Mr Murphy could put that up on screen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, next page.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: 2933. 2933, the next page, is the Dr Harkness note that we looked at a moment ago.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 2934 then.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy will get that up for us in a moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, so that's my ward round documented by Dr Ogden.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll just magnify that so we can all see it more clearly. Dr Ogden taking the notes that -- at 10 am she was with you, with the baby, when you reviewed the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "History overnight noted."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the history as documented by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes and Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And could you then, please, take us through the review?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So the first two lines, the V part, talks about baby is breathing in air and baby's saturations, the oxygen level in the body, is fine.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So the ventilation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Baby is not having any breathing issues.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next one. F stands for fluids, and:
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "Enteral feeds stopped overnight."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: What that means is, overnight, baby was getting some part of the feeds through the tube into the tummy and some part of the feeds through the drip and because they were having issues with the blood sugars, they stopped the feeds going into the tummy because the feeds which are going into the tummy need to be digested and absorbed. So to get a better control of the sugars, they have stopped the feeds and they were giving all the feeds — well, all the fluids through the drip.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not the feeds, the fluids.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Understood.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the fluids are total parenteral nutrition and the fluids volume was also increased from 150ml to 165ml per kilo per day, again because they were not able to control the -- they were not able to get the blood sugars back up.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right. So due to low blood sugar readings, there was a change in the regime of the provision of fluids --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- both in terms of the method and the extent?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you continue, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: BM, that is blood sugar, is low. So baby had three glucose boluses/dextrose boluses overnight. And the last bolus was given 30 minutes ago. So I suspect -- I'm not sure whether the 30 minutes refers to 10 o'clock or when I started the rounds. But the sugar now is 1.3.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And how would you assess a blood sugar reading of 1.3?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's still low.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Still too low?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And one plus -- I think it's dark milky aspirate from the stomach.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Then the next one, M, is for medication. So that documents the medicines the baby is on. They are caffeine, which we give for preterm babies to stimulate -- well, to make sure that they don't forget to breathe.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the baby is also on nystatin. That is mainly for preterm babies who are on in-dwelling plastic, so we give it to them to prevent fungal infections, so it's more of a preventative medicine. Cefotaxime, teicoplanin, those are the antibiotics which were changed the previous night when the baby became -- well, the sugars were low. So those two are antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: S. S... I'm not sure what S stands for. Okay, sepsis:
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "Re-screened overnight on cefotaxime and teicoplanin. CRP is less than 1, and W [that this is white blood cell count] is 3.6."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So CRP is a protein, which we measure as a marker of infection. Normally, it is less than 10. With infections it goes up quite high. But it can take time for the CRP to go up.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. So in summary, were the sepsis data, the sepsis readings, satisfactory or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: CRP, that is the initial reading, so it's not going to give us any more. So we normally measure another one in another 24 hours or so.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: White cell count is not elevated, so it is within -- probably I said in my statement that it's a little below the normal range, I can't remember now, but it's not elevated.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right. Let's move on to the next page then, please, 2935, where we get to some observations about the long line.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we are talking about -- L stands for line, so baby has long line in the right leg, which has been there for 7 days.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: N stands for neurology, which is baby's brain function.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So handles well. That is how baby is reacting to our touch, to the sounds and things like that: is the baby moving, moving all the limbs, crying or responding appropriately?
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So these notes that we're touching upon now, Dr Saladi, are these notes that record the observations that you made --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- upon examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Under "obs/examination", you repeat that the baby was handling well, that he was moving all four limbs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: All four limbs. Normal tone. So that is how -- we move the baby's sort of hands and feet and see whether they are limp, they are stiff, or they're normal.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next line refers to the heart sounds, so baby's heart sounds are well heard and there is no murmur.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: The next line refers to baby's breathing, so baby is -- no abnormal breath sounds and no increased work of breathing. The arrow up stands for increased. WOB stands for "work of breathing". The next line refers to the abdominal examination. No abdominal wall swelling.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Oedema refers to swelling. No abdominal wall erythema, which is redness or discolouration.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Pausing there, these elements of your examination up to this point were all satisfactory; is that correct or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you very much. But then we move to the next entry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So again, it refers to the abdomen:
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "Not distended/soft abdomen, and bowel sounds..."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: BS stands for bowel sounds. It says the bowel sounds are heard, which again is normal.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: It records the presence of --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Then?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Swelling in the right groin at the site of long line, plus indurated."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this baby had a long line on the right leg. So a long line is actually quite long, so it goes from the sort of foot into the groin and into the tummy. So this baby had a line like that put in in the right leg and the tip on the X-ray is there actually in the tummy.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: But we know that long lines can move as well, but I seem to have noticed a swelling in the right groin and I was wondering whether there is any swelling there which could come either because there is -- the line has -- the fluids from the line have leaked out into the tissues or signs of infection, those two are the possibilities.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: In this context, what does indurated mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The skin when you're feeling, it's a little bit more firm.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right. So would we be correct to conclude that this is an unsatisfactory observation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Moving on through the other observations.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The anterior fontanelle, the soft spot, is soft, as it should be. And the femorals, strong, as it should be.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Unable to palpate the right femoral, so obviously because there is a swelling there in the groin.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "The thigh, right, anterior/posterior, swollen and full."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So there is swelling on the front and the back of the thigh. And:
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "Heart rate has increased on palpation of the leg."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So that means when I was touching him, the heart rate goes up, suggesting -- that sort of suggests to us it's painful.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: On your examination and according to your conclusions was there a link between this apparent pain in the right thigh and the long line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That is correct.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So did you draft a plan accordingly?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Take us through the plan, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plan is stop the total parenteral nutrition via the long line. We also noticed that the glucose was low at the time of -- just before the round, so repeat bolus of dextrose, giving extra glucose solution. And move TPN to peripheral line -- that means in the lines that we have only mentioned long line, so maybe there was a plan to put a new peripheral line and give the glucose through that -- and a new long line.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: So pausing there, stop the TPN via the long line because the long line was causing a problem, discomfort --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: -- perhaps?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Repeat the bolus of dextrose. Would that be at the same time as stopping the TPN?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I suspect I might have, whilst I was doing this, if I have noticed this, because it's not documented there, but I
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: might have put a peripheral line and asked them to give the glucose through the peripheral line, that is a smaller line and then said, stop the long line and we'll put a new long line.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Right. The next line:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Move TPN to peripheral line."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: On a permanent basis or on a temporary basis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Temporary basis.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: On a temporary basis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Until we have the new long line.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Which takes us to the next entry of the plan:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "New long line."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that shorthand for "fit new long line" or "attach new long line"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: X-ray the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: X-ray abdomen with the long line position. And then continue antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Review feeding later. If settles after new long line can restart feeds."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Which to me -- settles means if the blood sugars settle, that means they are within the normal range, then we can restart feeds. And:
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: "Send long line tip for microscopy, culture and sensitivity."
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: To look for infection, bugs.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: To see what was the cause of the problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If there's any infection there, yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. So they are the instructions that you made.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then if we could just look further down the next page, please, Mr Murphy, 2936.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because one element of your plan was to undertake an X-ray to confirm that the long line was -- new long line was placed in a satisfactory position. If we go to 2936, please, we'll see the review of that X-ray, timed at 11.40 hours on 5 August. In short, did this review record that the long line was satisfactorily replaced?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Thank you. Dr Saladi, does that record the extent of your direct dealings with the baby [Baby F] on this date?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I probably would have checked or seen myself the Xray and then I probably would have gone to see the other babies if there is any further issues they might have discussed with me.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: That's all I would like to ask you about.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you remain there and answer any other questions, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Just a couple of points, Dr Saladi, if you could help us. Mr Murphy, could we go back to what we were looking at with Dr Saladi, which was page 2935, and just the plan?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: When you were talking -- can you see the entry that says "Move TPN to peripheral line"? You see that entry, do you, third line down?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: You said that maybe there was a plan to put in a new peripheral line and then you said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I might have put in a peripheral line and I asked the glucose to go through that."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In fact, do you recall precisely whether there was or there wasn't a peripheral line or do you not know, just looking at this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: All right. Thank you. The other thing I'd like it confirm, since you've referred to the question of testing the
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: tip, is can you confirm in fact [Baby F] did have an infection as it happens? Do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In the subsequent pages, there is a further entry that we did -- the CRP did go up and then we did grow a bug from the long line tip as well.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: That's right. In fact, can we scroll forwards to page 2938, Mr Murphy. If we go to the central entry marked 6 August 2015, 11.30, this is an entry by you, Dr Saladi. Do you agree we can see there the fourth line down:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "CRP increased from 1 to 40"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And up to 10 is the normal range. 40 would be consistent with an infection developing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And as you say also, it turned out when the tip of the long line was tested, there was bacteria on that consistent with infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which is usually -- bacteria which are normally there in the skin are also noted.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: And they get into it through the long line?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's possible.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the presence of those bacteria were confirmed on testing, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: SALADI

blocks.text: I only asked that for completeness because we talked about the test for infection, we don't know what happened, and I just wanted to establish that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, I have no re-examination. Does your Lordship have any questions for Dr Saladi?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't, thank you, Dr Saladi. I don't believe Dr Saladi will be giving evidence again.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: May I just double-check?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, please do.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.

blocks.text: Okay, thank you.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is, am I right, an antibiotic?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It is an antibiotic, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can then see, a minute later, administering sodium chloride?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: That would just be a flush, what we call a flush, so we've gone to give the penicillin. I will have -- or Belinda, whoever gave it, will have flushed first with a little bit of sodium chloride to check the line's patency and also to make sure that anything else is flushed through. We've then given the medication so you're not cross-mixing medications in the cannula or the line. Then we've given a little bit of a flush to make sure that all the medication has gone out of the line into the baby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it goes in before, then the antibiotics, then flushed through again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I think the next two tiles show that you then, having administered these particular medications, update the computer to that effect?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can we go to tile 139, please, next, only because we've been through these charts generally between 8 o'clock and midnight, they appear at each hourly entry and we have looked at them already. If we look behind 139 next. A blood gas record --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- from the unit? If we scroll down, please, to 4 August. We can see -- is that your signature on the right-hand side of that row?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It is for the bottom four entries that I can see.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just look at that entry first, please, timed at 11.32.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And reading across to the third column from the right — I think I can lead you on this -- this is the blood sugar level where you entered the blood sugar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: The 5.5.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And it's 5.5. Tell us how those readings are arrived at? Is there a sample taken from the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. So the C in the third column from the left indicates it was a capillary blood sample, so that will be a blood sample acquired from a little -- what we call a heel prick. We have special lancets that make an incision in the baby's heel. We then collect a small amount of blood into a capillary tube, that's then taken to the blood gas analyser, and that one little sample would give us that whole line of results.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Is there another way that blood sugar can be measured?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It can be collected by the same method, if need be, but into a little pot, for want of a better word, but then gets sent to the lab to be analysed. So there can be a slight difference between the two, but they usually correlate quite well and because it's a much smaller sample of blood then generally we will use the one on the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just excuse me a moment. When you take the blood gas readings, is there a printout of any sort or is it simply read off the machine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, there will be a little printout, if I remember rightly, because I've used several different blood gas machines since then. But I seem to remember this one did do a little printout that then we would take back and write the results on that chart.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Was there a means of doing it where there wasn't a printout or would there always be a printout from the machine? In other words, would both methods produce the printout?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Oh, if it went to the lab then that would be -- you'd be able to read that on the computer system --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- as well. This gas machine didn't talk to the computer system so it was recorded on the paper.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just looking across the line here, this entry with 5.5 on, is that all your handwriting right across the row?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I would say so, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. I ask simply because if we look at the very first figure 7 and the very last figure 7 across, one's got a little tail, the other hasn't, but it matters not perhaps.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: But then the seventh box where it says 26.7, that hasn't really got a tail either, has it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's all your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I think that is my handwriting. The last two columns look slightly less like my handwriting but I couldn't be certain.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. 5.5 in your experience, is that an acceptable blood sugar level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: That's a good blood sugar level, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. We've looked at the observations up until midnight. I'd like to look next, please, at tile 140.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm going to look next at tile 144, please and a document that lies behind it. I have taken you through the shift up to midnight and we had looked at the fluid balance chart and you'd told us that, by way of nutrition, at that stage [Baby F] was receiving TPN and expressed breast milk.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: With that in mind, could we scroll down, please, to days 7 and 8 on this particular chart. A chart you are familiar with?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I'm re-familiarising yourself.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Of course. Please take your time. Would you like to see the top of the form as well before we go on?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: If I could, yes, because it's some years now since I've worked there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we have heard how -- taking Dr Beech on the first line that you can see here by way of an example.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After initial Start-up, Maintenance -- Maintenance bags are prescribed to specific babies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Those prescriptions are sent to the -- please correct me if this is not consistent with your recollection -- they're sent to the pharmacy, usually in the morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Received on the ward, having been made up specifically in the pharmacy, in the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And stored in a fridge in the ward; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Marked for the specific baby subject to the prescription?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the target is to hang them round about midnight; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For a period of 48 hours ordinarily?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Unless something else happens?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. So can we look, please, at day 7, 4 August.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It gets complicated, I suppose, when it's either side of midnight, but certainly the form is dated 4 August.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: For now if we can ignore the fact there's a line through it, it's a prescription from Dr Beech, dated --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "time and date" -- I think that should say, it is just knocked out -- "begun" or "commenced". If we can lower that lower portion, Mr Murphy, please. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Time and date started"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this refers, does it, to a Babiven Maintenance bag started at 00.25 on 5 August?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you recognise the signatures underneath the column entitled "given by"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, I do. The top one is Lucy Letby and the lower one is myself.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You told us in respect of the computer that whoever's the co-signer or the inputter isn't always relevant to who did what; is the same true of this sort of form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. Completely one of us has signed first, it just happens to be Lucy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you have any recollection of this specific event?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. I suppose we're dealing, really, with both at the same time because if we look down at the second prescription, the time and date started remains the same. Are they the same two signatures --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- alongside?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, they are on the Babiven. The lipid underneath it, the bottom signature is mine. I think the top signature may be Belinda's.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Just looking at those two entries in tandem, just generally of hanging the bag, what does that tell you about, firstly, the time the bag was changed and what, if anything, changed thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So looking at that, I would say the bag was changed at 00.25, so just into 5 August --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- which would fit with that midnight. So if you look at the whole prescription, where it says daily millilitres per kilo, there's 57.9 there, so we know that he was having milk as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. If we read down, we can see 92.1 in the milk column.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. So the total added together would give you --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that would be his total fluid. So we know from that that he's having roughly two-thirds of his requirement enterally. So milk, which we know is mum's milk from the other chart, and then the rest of his fluid requirement is being given by the Babiven through the long line. And where the lipid is,
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: where Dr Beech has signed it and written "not required", she's prescribed it but they got prescribed in the morning, so basically she's prescribed that on the morning of the 4th. But by the time we came to put it up, he was over halfway on milk feeds, so we didn't as a rule give the lipid if they'd reached that amount of milk feeds --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- which is why we've written -- I believe that's Lucy's writing, not mine -- "not required" in the lipid.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's why it's not required.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So at the time the bag was hung at 00.25 on 5 August, the prescription, as it was, was correct with no requirement for lipid?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Then we might -- well, we will come to it in a moment. Did something then change for, firstly, the quantity to be amended, the constituents to be amended, and the lipid to be added?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, something has changed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We may come to that in a minute. Can we concentrate for now on the process of putting a bag up, as we've heard people put it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you mentioned a moment ago it would come via the long line.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is it physically hung up?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Physically hung up on a drip stand.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. All right. Is there a pump to maintain the flow and the pressure of the bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: There is, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that an Alaris pump?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I believe that was what we had at the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But there's certainly a pump through which it flows --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- in order to maintain the flow?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. You mentioned earlier that the bag was kept in the fridge once it was delivered to the ward.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So depending on what time it had been delivered, it's been in the fridge for a few hours; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So is there any process for removing it from the fridge or letting it warm again? What happens with the bag before it's hung?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I mean, it would be taken out of the fridge, maybe a little bit in advance because somebody might get it for you, not necessarily a set time in advance. He was on quite a small rate by that point so by the time it had travelled down the line it wouldn't be fridge-cold anyway.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So it would have time to warm up to room temperature?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Even if it was put up fairly quickly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Or you might get it out an hour in advance just to give it time to warm slightly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You mentioned that you wouldn't necessarily get it out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. I mean, because Chester at this time, we tried to change all our fluids around midnight, 48-hourly. It might be that there was more than one baby due fluids change. So if somebody went to the fridge, they might get two or three bags out and deliver the right bag to the right room or it might be whoever was allocated to look after that baby just went and got their bag out, but it could be somebody -- you'd say to somebody, "I need to change my fluids, could you get it for me as well?" There's no way of knowing, it would just depend on the workload.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we have heard there were keys for the fridge.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the fridge -- the keys would change hands from time to time; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it could be anyone who got the bag out of the fridge?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It wasn't necessarily the designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So would the bag, once it was retrieved from the fridge, go through a checking process?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. It would be, like all our medications, would be double-checked by -- two people would check it together.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And what would those checks, in the case of a Babiven bag, entail?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So the Babiven comes in a plastic bag that can't be seen through because it's light sensitive, so you take the bag out of that, check that the labels matched, that they were specifically for that baby, if it had the baby's names on. There was -- also what was in them might vary slightly from baby to baby depending on blood results. So you'd just check -- there would be a piece of paper that came with the bag and you'd check that everything married up so you were certain that was the bag for that baby at that time.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The piece of paper was that a copy of the prescription itself or was it something else?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, this was more... It was, from what I remember, the same as the label that was stuck on to the bag and the bag that covered the bag of fluids, just saying exactly what was in there in what amounts.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So obviously the first check would be the name of the baby --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- on the bag matched the name of the baby to whom you were about to administer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You would check the calculations and the amounts on the bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. We wouldn't necessarily check every little tiny calculation, but we'd just check that everything matched up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And two people would do that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To reduce the risk of an error, presumably?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would a nurse ever add anything to a Babiven bag at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So tell us then, please, about the process of hanging it. You told us there's a pump. You've checked -- the two of you who've checked, presumably would it have been the two who signed? Can you say that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Oh yes, that would be --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the two of you would have checked that it was the right bag and the numbers entered on the piece of paper that's in the bag with it, the covering bag. So physically the process, please, in a nutshell.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Because it was a long line, the one of us that was actually physically changing the bag would have sterile gloves on and would have washed because it's a central line, whereas a cannula is peripheral, so just want to be even more sure you don't introduce infection.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You've done your checks, you'd have your gloves on, the person checking with you would lift the old bag down -- you'd have stopped the infusion at this point because you're handling the line. And the old bag would be removed and the new bag would be connected.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. What would happen to an old bag?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: As a general rule it would be emptied and put in the bin.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So whatever liquid was remaining in would be disposed of?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the plastic went in the bin?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. So you stop the old bag. Is that by using the pump to stop the flow?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: You'd stop -- yes, the pump.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. And then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: You tend to clamp the line off as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then you would disconnect from the long line; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So it... It would depend. If you were just changing the bag of fluid, so the actual lines for the Babiven have a 96-hour filter on, so the actual line can stay connected to the baby for 96 hours/4 days maximum. But the bags need changing 48-hourly. So if it was just a bag change, you'd stop it, the line would remain attached to the baby. Whoever was changing it would have an alcohol wipe in each hand, so that it was sterile, so they weren't actually handling the line and the bag. They would pull the bag spike out of the bag, discard the old bag and attach the new bag.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: If it was at the end of -- you know, if that was the second bag that had been on that line, so you've come to the end of 96 hours, then you would run a whole new line, a whole new giving set through, and hang that and then the change would come at they baby, you would disconnect closer to the baby, the whole line, and reconnect the new one.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about giving sets.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The giving set, I think -- please correct me if I'm wrong -- connects the bag to the port into the long line; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You described it as a filter. Is that the same thing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So you've got your giving set and then the filter is a separate piece of line with the little filter built into it. So you connect that to the line so you --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So am I right, there's something between the giving set and the port?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's a filter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. Yes, it's about that long (indicating).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you indicate with your fingers about 6 inches?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: About 6 inches and it's got a little round white disc midway that is the filter.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Do you know what the filter is designed to filter out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Very small particles.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What is the filter made of, the device, the piece of kit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Plastic, the same as the giving set.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So you change the bag. Would you change a giving set with the bag as a matter of course?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Only if it was 96 hours since the whole giving set was changed, otherwise you'd just change --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's the giving set and the filter that last for 48 hours?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Lasts for 96 hours and the bag of fluid that lasts for 48 hours.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Can you tell, by looking at this form, whether the filter was 24, 48, 72 hours old? Any way to tell from the form?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Um... Not on that bit, no.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have the preceding ones, but they're all pretty well the same type of form.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Perhaps we could see the whole form, please, Mr Murphy. Perhaps if we have a look at the top half.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just want to see if there's anything you can see that indicates how long the filter or giving set has been in place.

blocks.text: Okay.

blocks.text: Thank you. Sorry, the observation chart. I was just going to look at that same period of time, the remainder of the shift on the observations chart, please.

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It may be fairly obvious but tell us what followed in the hours after midnight.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Well, as you can see, he'd been nice and stable for me in the evening and in fact the earlier part of the evening when I wasn't there, you can see his -- the recordings are all within a similar level that we're happy with. Then suddenly, at some point between midnight and 1 o'clock in the morning, he suddenly become tachycardic, so his heart rate's gone up, he's become tachypnoeic, so his respiration rate has gone up, his breathing rate has gone up, and both to a concerning level that would just -- that's why it's banded in yellow because that is -- at that point sort of you need to be reassessing, thinking about getting a review looking to see what else has changed. It's just there, the yellow band, as a prompt if you like.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see that the heart rate stays up in that yellow range for some hours thereafter --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- even when you (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Until 6 o'clock, it's beginning to come back down, isn't it? But then briefly dips but is consistently in the yellow for -- it's 12 hours, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- from 1 o'clock onwards; would that be fair to say?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. And then settled more quickly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've read in your note that you alerted Dr Harkness to the position. Is that the type of information that you'd have been concerned about and passing on to him?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, so he's -- I'd have contacted Dr Harkness, either bleeped him if he wasn't on the unit or if he was on the unit, just gone and had a discussion with him, and just to say sort of, [Baby F]'s been fine all night and now he's had a vomit and his heart rate's gone up and his respiration rate has gone up, can you come and have a look. blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: The blood sugar column.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.

blocks.text: And if we -- sorry, you were going to say something?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: To help correct something rather than to check line patency and --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. So can we just go through these in order because these probably draw together what the fluid chart was representing a little less accurately because of the time constraints in the boxes.

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Saline.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At 2.05 -- the second of your entries is timed at 2.05?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Oh yes. The other one's been prescribed first but given second, yes. So 3ml. That's, yes, 2ml per kilo of dextrose to bring his sugar up from that 0.8.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Then we've got some saline, a bolus of saline, at 02.55?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So that was mentioned. We...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we heard Dr Harkness explain why that was prescribed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Why that was given, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. Your next entry is 03.35, I think.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Which is saline again, which was -- we saw in my nursing notes some blood results that indicated he was dehydrated so we gave --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's the purpose of the second bolus, dehydration?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: That's the purpose of the second one, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So 03.50 is the infusion; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. That's the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The commencement of that?

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- additional 10%.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, we had a separate little bit that we could specifically --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right, okay. If I take you through it, you correct me if I get anything wrong:

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's I think what you described to us earlier:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They asked to be informed [not surprisingly] of any changes during the night."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They were updated after Dr Harkness' initial examination; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, review, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And they'd been present at the cot side since?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that was -- the first was 1.30, so they were there through the night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I can't remember exactly when and I can't remember if I went to get them, but somebody's gone because they'd asked, understandably, with [Baby E] the night before. blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Understandably very concerned and anxious. Kept up to date throughout. Seemed reassured that he's responded to fluid bolus. Understand that tachycardias can be caused by a combination of factors."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So this is all part, as the title suggests, of the family communication --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- discussing what's going on, what it might be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Parents also aware that [Baby F] is not stable enough for transfer today."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was that the plan?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Mum and dad were booked to have the boys at Ormskirk, but had been moved in utero to deliver at Chester, for bed pressures I presume. I know there'd been talk of them going back. I don't know whether there was a definite plan for them to go back the next day, but I think just because he was unstable I've said he's not going to be well enough to go today.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I can't remember the conversation exactly, but --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- but it's just part of keeping them as fully in the picture as possible.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we can then see mum then expresses views about staying where they are.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. If we could go to that other note, please, Mr Murphy, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is made, I think, around about the same time and is perhaps more to do with your responsibilities as a nurse. Very clearly indicates from 4.30, so we've had your note from 8 to 1, then 1 to 4.30, and this is the final third, if I can put it that way, of the shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Optiflow continues unchanged. Respiratory rate at 60"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Work of breathing satisfactory but remains tachycardic at 175 to 185."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So still just, casting our mind back to that chart, still skirting with that too high a level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. Just as I went off, he was sitting on the line between just about acceptable and the yellow band.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then this probably endorses what you said earlier:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Lively but generally settled and handled well."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he'd improved so far as his handling was concerned:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Phototherapy continues."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then this:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "LL patent but positional at times."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So long line. That's an abbreviation for long line. So it was patent, as in everything was flowing through it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember what limb this line was on, it'll be somewhere in the notes, but especially if they've been in for a few days — they're a very, very tiny line so it doesn't take much to occlude them. So if a bit of the line is over a joint or the ankle, it's positional that if the limb is in a -- changes position it might cause the pressure to go up on the line.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I break this down a little. Patent means open?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, the fluid's going through it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Occluded means blocked?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You couldn't use open and blocked?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Positional. Was there a problem with the line that you'd identified?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Not a problem as such. Like I say, these lines are minute, they are so thin, because they're threaded up a peripheral vein that is very small and the tip of them sits in a bigger vein. And then they've got fluid going through them but by the morning, as we've identified, there was a greater volume of fluid going through --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- which increases the pressure, if you like, going through that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- very narrow line. So they can be on a leg or on an arm and, depending where they are, if there were just a change in position, you know, the baby moves their foot and it's in a slightly different position because the line's so tiny, it can just cause it to narrow or dip more, which may then cause the pressure alarm on the pump to go off. So you check. So what I'm saying is that in certain positions it wasn't flowing quite as freely, but --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. I think you put at times.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: At times, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he had had some problems in other times, it was (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, which would make me think -- I can't remember which limb it was in, but if he moved his arm or his leg, wherever it was slightly, I might just need to go in and adjust his position slightly and check -- I'd always check the site to make sure it was still fine.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You said we identified it. Who did you identify it with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't know. I think I'm just talking generally.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would you have pointed it out to Ms Simcock perhaps?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't think specifically. I think that's just me talking in general terms as a nurse.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Then you've summarised:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "TPN/lipid, 10% dex to continue through it."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which follows on from the charts we've been looking at, and you put down one of the repeat blood glucose results?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which I think was the last one before you went off duty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Can we turn next please to tile 222. If we can go into these messages, please. These are a reproduction of some messages, WhatsApps specifically, between yourself and Ms Letby. Do you have any recollection of receiving that message now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. Not specifically.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It wouldn't be an unusual message to receive.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Did you hear what [Baby F]'s sugar was at 8?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is at 08.47, after you've finished your shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So do you know who she's talking about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I would guess [Baby F].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Look at the next message, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have gone off duty by this point presumably?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I must have handed over and gone before there was another sugar done. I could see on the chart there was one done not long after the end of my shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So at 8 o'clock when it was done, some people still there, some people not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I'd gone, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Next one, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the result?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can go on again. It's all right, don't worry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just wondered what you meant by:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I feel awful leaving it 3 hours."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you remember what you were thinking?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: We'd had an okay result. As I said, we take blood sugars from the baby's heels, the capillary samples, we make a little incision each time in their heel to take blood. So he's obviously had a lot of samples taken overnight. Heels can become quite sore.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So sometimes it's a balance of: I've had a good result so I'll just maybe leave it a little bit longer before I do it... It's balancing -- everything is a balance.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Why did you feel awful?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Because it was too low.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So I was wondering if I'd done it an hour earlier it might not have been as low.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Blaming yourself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Next message, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Is that to me?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's to you from Ms Letby. You told us that his fluids had been increased to that 165 per kilo --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- in the early hours of the morning. Then she makes a similar observation to you about the heels.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I mean (inaudible) heels sometimes these little -- I mean, you are talking about a little baby and you've got to do it on specific parts of the heels, so there's a lot to consider.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is the capillary sample you were telling us about before?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You have to pierce the heel?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, it's more of a little cut, almost like a little paper cut. It's not paper, but that's almost what it looks like. If you're doing multiple ones, then they've not got very big heels and...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Understood. Next message, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In fact that's the last message.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. Okay, let's have a look at that. So this is your response at 09.09:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Exactly. He'd had so much handling."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you're agreeing with the point you just made to us:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No, something not right. HR and sugars."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Something wasn't right, was it? His heart rate was high and his sugars were low. That's an indication to me that in a baby that's been stable, something's changed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. All right, thank you. Next message, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think there's a few more.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ms Letby to you:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs came so hopefully they'll get him sorted."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Next, please. That's Ms Letby again:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "He's a worry [though]."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I think you're replying to both of those:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Hope so."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In respect of Dr Gibbs; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, I would.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And agreeing that he's a worry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I mean, it was sudden.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You said it was sudden?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, your voice dropped ever so slightly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, it was sudden.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Hope you sleep well."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, even if I got off on time, I didn't get in until gone half 8.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Carry on, please. Now, you were due to be on the next night, is that right, because you told us earlier this was your first night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- which you have just been talking about.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. There is actually a third way, which is capillary as well, which is a little blood glucose monitor that would just give you a blood glucose, which you might use if you didn't --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- want any other tests doing at the time.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I was going to ask you.

blocks.text: Right.

blocks.text: NURSE A: So again, to conserve blood, if you didn't need any other tests, you would use one of those.

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, it would only do a blood glucose.

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
